content: The cardiotocograph, also referred to as an electronic fetal monitor (EFM) or external fetal monitor, is a medical device used to monitor the well-being of a pregnant woman, particularly during the third trimester of pregnancy. This device simultaneously measures the fetal heart rate and uterine contractions, if present, using two separate disc-shaped transducers placed on the woman’s abdomen. An ultrasound transducer is responsible for detecting the fetal heartbeat, while a pressure-sensitive transducer, known as a tocodynamometer (or toco), measures the strength and frequency of uterine contractions. The cardiotocograph was invented by Dr. Orvan Hess and Dr. Edward Hon. When this device is used during the third trimester to assess fetal well-being, the procedure is referred to as a non-stress test (NST). A positive result in an NST is indicated by a reactive non-stress test, which means that the fetal heart rate increased (accelerated) by at least 15 beats per minute for a duration of at least 15 seconds on at least two occasions within a 20-minute period. During labor, the use of the cardiotocograph is referred to as a stress test. When this practice was first introduced, it was anticipated to reduce the incidence of fetal demise during labor and to lower the rates of cerebral palsy (CP). In recent years, however, there has been some debate regarding the utility of the cardiotocograph in low-risk pregnancies. Critics argue that over-reliance on this test has led to an increase in misdiagnoses of fetal distress, which in turn has contributed to a rise in cesarean deliveries, some of which may be unnecessary.
